description: Roslyn analyzers for Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection that catch captive dependencies, DI scope leaks, BuildServiceProvider misuse, service locator usage, and unresolvable services at compile time in ASP.NET Core and .NET applications.
releaseNotes: **DI003 fixer renamed user methods**: the lifetime rewrite's fix-target walk matched any ancestor invocation whose method name merely contained "Singleton"/"Scoped"/"Transient", so a user helper like `Mappers.MapScopedValue(...)` wrapping the diagnosed resolution was renamed instead of the registration — non-compiling output. Rewrite targets now require the bound method to live on the framework's own registration types (`ServiceCollectionServiceExtensions`, `ServiceCollectionDescriptorExtensions`, `ServiceCollectionHostedServiceExtensions`, or `ServiceDescriptor` in the MEDI namespaces) — a namespace-only check would still have matched user helpers declared inside `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` for extension discoverability. | **DI003 own-scope factory false positive**: a factory that creates and provably disposes its own scope (`using var scope = sp.CreateScope(); var seed = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<…>();`) performs one-time scoped setup — the resolved instance does not outlive the factory call, so nothing is captive. Resolution receivers are now classified (framework `CreateScope`/`CreateAsyncScope` surface only — user overloads declared in the MEDI namespace do not qualify; any dispose before the last use of the resolved value kills the proof even for `using var` scopes; only same-execution-context resolutions qualify — a nested lambda resolving from the outer factory's scope runs after disposal and still reports; an explicit `Dispose()` only proves cleanup when it dominates the resolution — conditional, nested-lambda, or fire-and-forget `DisposeAsync()` calls do not) and the suppression additionally requires the resolved instance not to escape into the product — provably-safe derived values (primitives, enums, and strings, like `seed.Config` — arbitrary structs may carry the instance in a field and do not qualify) may flow onward — a reference-typed member result such as `seed.GetSelf()` may carry the instance and still reports — while the instance itself (`return new Singleton(seed)`), a method group capturing it (`seed.DoWork`), or a closure over it in a nested lambda (`() => seed.Config`) still reports; the explicit dispose must also run after the last use of the resolved value with no return/throw/jump in between, so consuming the service from an already-disposed scope — or leaking it through an early exit — is never blessed, while the `try { … return …; } finally { scope.Dispose(); }` idiom is honored because finally always runs. An undisposed factory scope also stays reported because the scope and its scoped instances live as long as the product.
